title: Automated Employment Decision Tools: Frequently Asked Questions
pub: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
author: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection

dom.t: Hiring audits: Disclosure cannot guarantee nondiscrimination

st.t: Employment screening: Audits reveal bias without remedying it
st.an: DCWP’s guidance directly supports the synthesis: Local Law 144 imposes audit-and-notice procedures but does not treat an audit as proof of fairness or prescribe remediation. It instead leaves necessary responses to applicable anti-discrimination law and separately distinguishes procedural enforcement from discrimination claims.
qs: The Law requires employers and employment agencies to do a bias audit; however, the Law does not require any specific actions based on the results of a bias audit.
Employers and employment agencies must comply with all relevant Anti-Discrimination laws and rules to determine any necessary actions based on the results of a bias audit.

st.t: Hiring audits: Disclosure cannot guarantee nondiscrimination
st.an: The DCWP guidance directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: Local Law 144 imposes audit, disclosure and notice procedures but does not prescribe corrective action or itself guarantee nondiscrimination; employers must separately determine their obligations under applicable antidiscrimination law. It also supports the cluster’s coverage, methodology and employer-responsibility points, though it does not establish the no-alternative-process point.
qs: The Law requires employers and employment agencies to do a bias audit; however, the Law does not require any specific actions based on the results of a bias audit.
Employers and employment agencies must comply with all relevant Anti-Discrimination laws and rules to determine any necessary actions based on the results of a bias audit.

mo.t: Automated decisions: Notice and recourse remain distinct rights
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks

kp.k: NYC conditions automated employment decisions on audits and notices
kp.d: DCWP describes Local Law 144 of 2021 as prohibiting covered AEDT use without a bias audit and required notices. The law took effect on January 1, 2023, with enforcement beginning July 5, 2023. These are regulatory requirements for employment decision tools, not findings about changes in legal work. Although the supplied heading labels the source 2026, the FAQ pages are dated 06/29/2023.
qs: The Law prohibits employers and employment agencies from using an automated employment decision tool (AEDT) in New York City unless they ensure a bias audit was done and provide required notices.
It took effect on January 1, 2023. Enforcement begins on July 5, 2023.

kp.k: Coverage depends on technology and decision-making influence
kp.d: The FAQ defines an AEDT through three cumulative conditions: use of machine learning, statistical modeling, data analytics or AI; assistance with employment decisions; and substantial assistance to or replacement of discretionary decision-making. It describes the relevant techniques as generating predictions or classifications and identifying inputs, their relative importance and other parameters to improve accuracy.
qs: Substantially assists or replaces discretionary decision-making.
A prediction includes but is not limited to an assessment of a candidate’s fit for the job or likelihood of success.
A classification is an assignment of an observation to a group, such as categorizations based on skill sets or aptitude.

kp.k: Territorial coverage includes remote jobs associated with NYC offices
kp.d: Covered use includes jobs located at least part time in an NYC office, fully remote jobs associated with an NYC office, and use by employment agencies located in NYC. For agencies outside NYC, the stated NYC job-location conditions must apply. The FAQ distinguishes this territorial scope from the residency condition for candidate notices.
qs: The Law applies only to employers and employment agencies that use an AEDT “in the city.”
The job is fully remote but the location associated with it is an office in NYC.
Job candidates who are New York City residents must receive notice that the employer or employment agency uses an AEDT.

kp.k: Screening is covered; pre-application outreach is excluded
kp.d: The requirements reach substantial AEDT assistance at any stage of hiring or promotion assessment, not merely final decisions. Resume-bank scanning, outreach and invitations to apply fall outside the requirements when the person has neither applied for a specific position nor is an employee being considered for promotion.
qs: The Law defines employment decision more broadly to include screening.

If employers or employment agencies use an AEDT to substantially help them assess or screen candidates at any point in the hiring or promotion process, they must comply with the Law’s requirements before using an AEDT.

If AEDT use is to assess someone who is not an employee being considered for promotion and who has not applied for a specific position for employment, the bias audit and notice requirements do not apply.

kp.k: Annual independent audits measure demographic selection and scoring disparities
kp.d: The required bias audit is an impartial evaluation by an independent auditor, minimally calculating selection or scoring rates and impact ratios across sex, race/ethnicity and intersectional categories. Employers and agencies may rely on an audit for only one year. Categories representing less than 2% of audit data may be excluded from required calculations, but all other categories must remain.
qs: At a minimum, an independent auditor’s evaluation must include calculations of selection or scoring rates and the impact ratio across sex categories, race/ethnicity categories, and intersectional categories.
Employers and employment agencies can only rely on a bias audit for one year from the date it was conducted.
If a category represents less than 2% of the data used for the bias audit, it can be excluded from the required calculations.

kp.k: Audit results do not trigger specified corrective actions
kp.d: Local Law 144 requires an audit but does not prescribe particular action when results appear to indicate disparate impact. DCWP explicitly qualifies this by noting that federal, state and NYC anti-discrimination obligations still apply and may require action. DCWP handles audit and notice compliance, while discrimination claims are referred to the NYC Commission on Human Rights.
qs: The Law requires employers and employment agencies to do a bias audit; however, the Law does not require any specific actions based on the results of a bias audit.
Employers and employment agencies must comply with all relevant Anti-Discrimination laws and rules to determine any necessary actions based on the results of a bias audit.
DCWP will refer any claims of discrimination to the Commission.

kp.k: Public audit summaries must disclose results and data provenance
kp.d: Employers and agencies must publish the most recent audit summary and the AEDT distribution date on their employment website section or through an active hyperlink. The summary must disclose the audit date, source and explanation of data, the number assessed in an unknown category, applicant or candidate counts, selection or scoring rates and impact ratios for all categories.
qs: Distribution date is the date employers and employment agencies began using the AEDT.
The source and explanation of the data used to conduct the bias audit.
The number of individuals the AEDT assessed that fall within an unknown category.
The number of applicants or candidates, the selection or scoring rates, as applicable, and the impact ratios for all categories.

kp.k: Historical data is standard; pooled audits have reliance conditions
kp.d: Audits ordinarily must use historical data collected during actual candidate or promotion assessment. An employer or agency may rely on an audit pooling historical data across users of the same AEDT only if it contributed its own historical data or is using the tool for the first time. Contributors need not hire or promote for the same type of position. Limits on historical data, including region or time period, should be explained.
qs: “Historical data” is the data collected during an employer’s or employment agency’s use of an AEDT to assess candidates for employment or employees for promotion.
They provided historical data from their use of the AEDT to the independent auditor conducting the bias audit.
It is the first time they are using the AEDT.
There is no additional requirement that the companies providing historical data used the AEDT to hire or promote for the same type of position.
If the historical data was limited in any way, including to a specific region or time period, the audit should explain why.

kp.k: Test-data flexibility accompanies a ban on demographic inference
kp.d: Imputed or inferred demographic information cannot be used in a bias audit. Where historical data is insufficient for a statistically significant audit, other employers’ historical data or test data may be used. DCWP sets neither a specific statistical-significance requirement nor requirements for test data, leaving the insufficiency determination to the independent auditor while requiring disclosure of why test data was used and its source and description.
qs: Imputed or inferred data cannot be used to conduct a bias audit.
DCWP has not set a specific requirement for statistical significance.
If an independent auditor determines there is insufficient historical data to conduct a statistically significant bias audit, test data may be used to conduct the bias audit.
The summary of results of the bias audit must explain why test data was used and include the source and description of the data.
To allow for flexibility and development of best practices in this rapidly developing field, DCWP has not set requirements for test data.

kp.k: Auditor independence excludes employment, involvement and financial conflicts
kp.d: DCWP does not require auditor approval. Independence requires objective and impartial judgment and excludes those working for the tool-using employer or agency or its developer/distributor, those previously involved in using, developing or distributing the AEDT regardless of current employment, and those with direct or material indirect financial interests in the relevant organizations.
qs: The Law does not require independent auditors to be approved by DCWP.
An independent auditor is someone who exercises objective and impartial judgment in the performance of a bias audit.
Were involved in using, developing, or distributing the AEDT regardless of where they work currently.
Have a direct financial interest or a material indirect financial interest in the employer or employment agency that will use the AEDT or the vendor that developed or distributed the AEDT.

kp.k: Employers retain responsibility even when vendors arrange audits
kp.d: Responsibility for ensuring a pre-use bias audit rests with employers and employment agencies, not the vendor that created the tool. Vendors may nevertheless commission an independent audit and coordinate data collection; this does not transfer the user's compliance responsibility.
qs: The vendor that created the AEDT is not responsible for a bias audit of the tool.
A vendor can have an independent auditor do a bias audit of its tool.
The Law does not prohibit a vendor from having a bias audit done or coordinating the collection of data to use to conduct a bias audit.
Employers and employment agencies are ultimately responsible for ensuring a bias audit was done before using an AEDT.

kp.k: Advance notices disclose tool use and assessed characteristics
kp.d: NYC-resident employees and candidates must receive notice of AEDT use and the qualifications or characteristics assessed, including instructions for requesting reasonable accommodation under other laws, 10 business days before use. Permitted channels include job postings, mail and email, with non-position-specific website notices for applicants and written policies or procedures for promotion candidates. Website notice permits use after 10 business days regardless of when a particular job was posted.
qs: Employers and employment agencies must notify employees and job candidates who are residents of New York City that they are using an AEDT and the job qualifications or characteristics the AEDT will assess.
Include in the notice instructions to request a reasonable accommodation under other laws.
Provide the notice 10 business days before using an AEDT.
Employers and employment agencies can begin using an AEDT 10 business days after posting notice on their website regardless of when a specific job posted.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: DCWP describes how automated hiring and promotion tools trigger audit, disclosure and notice obligations, rather than predicting changes to legal services or employment levels.
pts.d: In this cross-domain source, DCWP states that covered automated employment decision tools (AEDTs) use machine learning, statistical modeling, data analytics or AI to help make employment decisions and substantially assist or replace discretionary decision-making. Their outputs can predict job fit or success or classify candidates by skills or aptitude. Covered use includes screening, not just final decisions. Local Law 144 prohibits covered use without a bias audit and required notices. The independent audit must calculate selection or scoring rates and impact ratios across sex, race/ethnicity and intersectional categories; users must publish a results summary and the tool's distribution date. DCWP expressly distinguishes these procedural requirements from a requirement to act on audit findings: the law itself mandates no specific response to apparent disparate impact, although other anti-discrimination laws remain applicable. The source offers no prediction that these obligations will reduce bias, improve hiring accuracy or displace workers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on DCWP's regulatory authority and its explanation of Local Law 144 and implementing rules, not empirical findings about AI's effects.
pts.d: DCWP identifies itself as the enforcing agency and cites The Rules of the City of New York for definitions, audit calculations and data requirements. No datasets, measured effects, benchmark results or enforcement cases are reported. The FAQ specifies evidence to be used in future compliance audits: historical tool-use data is the default; pooled historical data and test data are permitted under stated conditions; imputed or inferred demographic information cannot be used. DCWP has set neither a specific statistical-significance requirement nor requirements for test data, instead requiring explanations of data sources and use. Categories representing less than 2% of audit data may be excluded from required calculations. These are methodological rules and qualifications, not evidence that any particular tool is fair or effective.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The FAQ describes a regime effective January 1, 2023, with enforcement beginning July 5, 2023, annual audits and notice at least 10 business days before use.
pts.d: Although the supplied document heading labels the source 2026, the reproduced FAQ pages are dated June 29, 2023; the operative dates stated in the text are in 2023. An audit must precede covered use and remain no more than one year old. Notice must precede use by 10 business days. Geographic coverage includes jobs located at least partly in an NYC office, fully remote jobs associated with an NYC office, and use by NYC employment agencies; agencies outside NYC are covered when the stated job-location conditions hold. Notice obligations concern NYC-resident applicants and employees. Coverage applies to assessment of applicants for specific positions or employees considered for promotion, not general resume-bank scanning, outreach or invitations to apply. Reliance on pooled audits requires contributing the user's historical data or being a first-time user. Test data is allowed when historical data is insufficient for a statistically significant audit, with an explanation of its use and provenance.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Employers and employment agencies bear compliance responsibility; candidates receive disclosures; independent auditors perform evaluations; vendors may facilitate but do not inherit users' obligations.
pts.d: DCWP assigns ultimate responsibility for ensuring an audit to employers and employment agencies, even when a vendor arranges an independent audit or coordinates data collection. Auditors must exercise objective and impartial judgment; employment relationships, involvement in using, developing or distributing the tool, and specified financial interests disqualify independence. DCWP does not approve auditors. NYC-resident job applicants and employees must be told about AEDT use and the qualifications or characteristics assessed, with instructions for requesting reasonable accommodation under other laws. Public audit summaries disclose category-level results, data sources and unknown-category counts. People may complain to DCWP about audit or notice violations; discrimination claims belong with the NYC Commission on Human Rights. No separate impact on lawyers, law firms or legal-service markets is asserted.
